statement: The second half of the lecture designs Slack's real-time communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now what we'll do is we'll design Slack real-time communication.

statement: The teacher dislikes the framing 'design Slack' (the entire product); instead pick one part and do it really well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So one thing that I kind of hate is how when people put out, they say design Slack, entire Slack you will design, right?

statement: Scope: Slack real-time communication, text only - nothing more - i.e. the kind of messages seen on Teams, Insta, Facebook; kept simple to understand the foundational building blocks, the nitty-gritties and how design decisions are made.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: nothing more, only text-based real-time communication

statement: Requirements: one organization on Slack with multiple users (employees) and multiple channels; a user can direct-message another user or post a message in a channel; the chat must be real time; historical messages can be scrolled (e.g. scroll a channel back to older messages).
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User can direct message another user or can put a message in a channel. The chat needs to be real time...

statement: The same real-time architecture can be used to build many things: multiplayer games, real-time chat, interactions, real-time polls, creative tools.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This same thing can be used to build ton of stuff, multiplayer games, real time chat, interactions, real time polls, creative tools and whatnot.

statement: Plan for the design: brainstorm channels, messages, checkpoints and real-time communication, then reach WebSockets and scale them; the key highlight is how each decision is made rather than drawing boxes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll kick off our brainstorming and we'll cover all these parts, channels, messages, checkpoints, and real-time communication.

statement: Jumping directly to WebSockets is not a good idea; cover the basics first, then come to WebSockets, then scale them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Directly jumping to WebSockets is not a good idea.

statement: Start a design brainstorm with the simple stuff: the schema is the easiest thing to start with, limited to the required features only.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's start with simple stuff. Schemas. That's the easiest thing to start with, right?

statement: Designing a schema (entities and their attributes) does not mean using a relational database; the database is picked afterwards, depending on the guarantees wanted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It depends on the kind of guarantees we want to put and then we pick the database.

statement: A student's first schema: a users table (ID, name, optional nickname), a channels table (organization ID, channel ID) and a messages table holding the channel ID in which the user sent the message; the teacher accepted it and asked for more.
detail: Teacher: "That's okay. What else?"
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So user with their ID, name, and if they have like some nickname, which they can have.

statement: The schema must store which users are part of which channel; a student proposed a 'membership' table for this, and the teacher praised the name (the student came up with it without seeing the board) as brilliant.
detail: Teacher asked: how do you know which user is part of which channel? Student 1: a membership table.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: how do you know which user are part of which channel? You need to store it somewhere, right?

statement: When designing a schema, everything should be an entity named as a noun wherever possible; a noun gives the table a persona of its own.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever you're designing a good schema, everything has to be an entity, has to be a noun.

statement: Many people would name the user-to-channel mapping table 'user_channel'; the teacher is against this: it is the easy way to name things, but it says nothing (if tomorrow you map three things, would you name it user_channel_message?).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because this is the easy way to name stuff, user channel. But what is user channel?

statement: A noun name like 'membership' makes extension natural: you can easily add more columns to it, whereas with a name like 'user_channel' you do not think of adding another attribute.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: as soon as you give it a noun, let's say membership, it becomes very natural to add new columns to that

statement: A student proposed a messages table with the sender, the message text, and both a channel ID and a receiver user ID, one of which is always null (channel messages vs direct messages); the teacher asked what the disadvantage of this is.
detail: Corrected in the following items: nullable either/or columns allow orphan rows.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So here you'll have channel ID also and the receiver ID also.
flags: check: diarization seam at 01:05:49 - the student's answer may start in the teacher's paragraph

statement: Allowing either of two columns (channel ID or receiver ID) to be null also allows inserting a row where both are null due to some glitch, which becomes an orphan row problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: insert a row where both the columns can be null due to some glitch. So which means that would become an orphan row problem.

statement: A student proposed two separate tables, one for channel messages and one for direct messages.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: migrations become difficult, since adding a new attribute to messages means adding it to both tables.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But then your migrations would be difficult.

statement: A student considered storing the receiver ID as an array of all receiving users, but noted it breaks when users are added to the channel; the teacher said there has to be a better way.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: having a receiver ID as a array of all the receiver users
flags: check: diarization seam - "again to this ID" may be Student 1's

statement: A student proposed from/to columns where 'to' is either a channel ID or a user ID, distinguished by a prefix (e.g. 'CH-' vs 'usr-').
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: every query would need string processing to decide whether to join with channel or with user - a poor implementation that prevents efficient queries.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Then you join it with channel, otherwise you join it with user. That's a poor implementation.

statement: A student proposed adding a receiver-type enum column (channel or user) next to the 'to' column.
detail: Correction: The teacher said these are all variations of the same thing: 'to' can no longer have a foreign-key check, because it may point to a channel or to a user.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: cannot have a foreign key check on to, which says that it's a foreign relationship to channel, right?
flags: check: diarization seam - "but now what would happen is now you" (01:09:37) may be the Teacher's

statement: A polymorphic 'to' column also forces many ifs and elses into the business logic (if this then this, else that), making it complicated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in our business logic we have to have so many ifs and else's

statement: A student suggested the message should not know where it is going (routing is control information, maybe handled in code rather than the DB).
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: without storing the 'to' information you cannot render all the messages of a channel.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: How will you render all the channels or all the messages of a channel, if you don't store to information over here, right?
flags: check: diarization seam - "then I'll say Alexa, go on" is likely the Teacher's

statement: A student proposed giving two users who DM a common channel and also treating it as a topic in a publisher-subscriber model.
detail: Correction: The teacher kept the DM-as-channel part but called the publisher-subscriber addition an unnecessary complication ('focus on the first part').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So good, and then you just added publisher subscriber, unnecessary complication.
flags: check: Student 2 label at 01:11:23 may be a different student from 01:10:15

statement: Good schema: model direct messages as channels with two people; this piggybacks on existing stuff (channels and messages) instead of special-casing DMs.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the way we model this is, your DMs are channeled with two people

statement: This is how Slack's API works: to DM a particular user you first create a channel with that user and then write on it; it is rendered as a direct message in the UI, but behind the scenes it is a channel.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you ever use Slack API and you want to DM a particular user, you first have to create a channel with that user

statement: At the end a DM and a channel message are just a message with a sender and a receiver; only the rendering differs on the UI side, not the way it is stored.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Receiver, the rendering part is different on the UI side, but the way you are storing it

statement: Always see if you can have a generalized way of storing things rather than specific cases (if this go here, if that go there); ifs and elses are the worst when it comes to databases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Ifs and elses are the worst when it comes to databases.

statement: The channel table gets a type field (group, user/DM or regular channel); messages carry a channel ID pointing to the channel, and the type lets the UI render DMs in the bottom half and channels in the top half.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with this type you can render it on the top half or on the bottom half, because direct messages are on the bottom half.

statement: Messages carry a creation timestamp (created_at); through the channel you can iterate over all its messages to scroll historical messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would have a timestamp field on when it was created, message created at or something.

statement: Resulting schema: users; channels (with type); membership information in the membership table; messages pointing to a channel.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Store membership information over here. Channel information over here

statement: Because the table is named 'membership' (a noun), it can store a checkpoint: for a user in a channel, the point up to which the user has read messages.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now what you can do is you can actually store the checkpoint over here.

statement: The checkpoint drives what users see in the UI: the unread message count, 'you last read until here', and on clicking a channel with a hundred new messages, being taken to that point.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You see the unread message count. You see you last read until here.

statement: Naming the table 'membership' automatically triggers your brain to add more attributes (e.g. read-till point, active for this time, how a user interacts with the channel), giving scope for extension; the 'channel' can be a channel, a user or a DM.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It automatically triggers your brain to think that I can add more attributes to that.

statement: Whenever a user opens a channel, the checkpoint moves to the bottom (last message read); it can store a timestamp or a message ID, depending on the implementation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And whenever you open a channel, the checkpoint moves to the bottom of it.

statement: Checkpoint granularity is a choice: time-level ('I read till this time') or message-level ('I read till this message').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you either want to operate on the time level granularity that I read till this time, or you want to operate on message level granularity

statement: Other user-channel interactions also go into the membership table: muted, favorited, notification type settings; no separate table for favorites is needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: User favorited a channel, add it over here. No need to have another table to store favorites.

statement: Because it holds every interaction a user has with a channel, the membership table becomes the key table of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why this table becomes that key thing in the system, right?

statement: Two key takeaways of the schema discussion: name things as nouns, and piggyback on existing entities rather than having ifs and elses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One key takeaways, noun-based stuff. How you are piggybacking and not having ifs and else's.

statement: High-level design assumption: messages are stored in a relational database which is sharded.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are storing the data, the messages in a relational database which is sharded.

statement: For Slack you don't typically need a non-relational database, because the frequency of messages is not very high; a simple sharded relational database would work, since all you need is to store ingested messages and scroll through them.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You don't typically need to store it in non-relational over here because the frequency of messages is not very high.

statement: You can also choose a non-relational database like MongoDB or Cassandra for the messages; no one stops you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can also choose to store it on a non-relational database like MongoDB or Cassandra.

statement: Even a relational database does a very good job of storing chat messages, given that it is partitioned and sharded.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even relational database would do a very good job over here, obviously given that it is partitioned and sharded.

statement: Cassandra-like databases are very ingestion heavy and suit very high-ingestion systems such as real-time chat messages at scale (WhatsApp, Instagram, Tinder).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Cassandra like databases, where it is very ingestion heavy, you can use it to build very high ingestion system

statement: An enterprise application has a different use case: no huge amount of messages is exchanged; people chit-chat sometimes, but not everyone sends hundreds and thousands of messages, because they are there to work.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for enterprise application the use case would be a little different because there is no huge amount of messages being exchanged.

statement: Picking a database depends on the product and the requirement, not on your affinity to a particular stack.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why picking a database depends on the product and the requirement, not your affinity to a particular stack.

statement: For enterprise chat there is no hard and fast rule (MySQL, Cassandra, Mongo, any database) because the scale is not huge, but sharding and partitioning are definitely needed: add more partitions, put a bunch of enterprise customers on a particular database; no fancy NoSQL database is needed.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can add more partitions, put a bunch of enterprise customers on a particular database and whatnot.

statement: Whenever you pick something, understand why you are picking it: what use case are you solving?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So whenever you are picking something, understand where you are picking it from. What's the use case that you are solving?

statement: Instagram Messenger vs Slack: for Instagram Messenger the teacher would pick Cassandra (a high-ingestion-rate database), because everyone is chit-chatting and all users are in one database; for an enterprise app with formal messaging even MySQL works, as long as it is partitioned and sharded (Cassandra is still allowed).
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But if you are building Instagram Messenger, I would have gone for Cassandra. Because there everyone is chit-chatting.

statement: Whatever database is picked (MongoDB, MySQL, Cassandra), the overall schema looks very similar.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you pick MongoDB, MySQL, Cassandra, any, the overall schema would look something very similar to this.

statement: Design question: when a user sends a message to a channel, how should it reach and be persisted in the database - through the (normal) API servers or through a WebSocket?
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when a user sends a message, how should that message be persisted in this database?

statement: A student proposed a WebSocket connection between users and server for sending, because the server must also push to clients.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: receiving needs WebSocket (so people don't have to refresh), but that does not mean sending must also go over WebSocket.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But this does not mean that sending also needs to be done on WebSocket.

statement: Just because you have a WebSocket connection does not mean you have to use it for everything; think about the guarantees you get or lose when using WebSockets.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just because you have it does not mean you have to use it.

statement: Users have connections with both normal API servers and WebSocket servers, so a message could be sent via either.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I agree that user would have connections with normal API servers also. And WebSockets servers also.

statement: A student proposed sending over WebSocket to save per-message overhead compared with REST, since chat is frequent communication.
detail: Correction: The teacher pushed back: why does REST exist at all if WebSocket were always better, and is Slack really as frequent as Instagram Messenger? You do not receive many messages on Slack/Teams.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You're saying frequent, is Slack really as frequent as your Instagram Messenger? Think about it.
flags: check: diarization seam - "trying to save that overhead?" (01:24:45) continues the teacher's question

statement: Slack's customers are enterprises; for them persistence of messages is more critical than saving per-message overhead.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Is persistence of message more important? Right.

statement: Not everything needs to be done in an instant: everything has an overhead, and if WebSocket were always the answer everyone would use it for everything, which is not happening; there must be better reasoning for choosing REST or WebSocket.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let me just use WebSocket for everything. Right. But that's not happening.

statement: A student said the expectation is that a sent message shows to other users immediately.
detail: Correction: The teacher redirected: not the expectation, what you actually see as a user - on Slack the message is not immediately posted (try sending yourself a Slack message).
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Not expectation. What do you see as a user? You don't see message immediately getting posted.

statement: A student said they would 'definitely' choose WebSocket for sending, since a REST call needs a handshake and a TCP connection.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected: then the entire world should use only WebSockets - why have normal API servers or spin up Spring Boot instances at all?
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Then the entire world should use just WebSockets for everything.
flags: check: speaker of 01:27:03 - teacher called on 'Summit' but the turn is labelled Student 1

statement: Receiving messages has to be done over WebSocket; the debate is only about how messages are sent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Receiving has to be done over WebSocket. I'm not denying that at all.

statement: Think of the guarantees you need to provide to your customer (as Slack) when a message is put out; the architecture follows from them.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: think of the guarantees that you need to provide to your customer.

statement: On Slack a sent message first appears grey and then turns black: there is a visible delay after hitting send, a clear indication that sending is not extreme real time.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: First, it's like you see it gray and then it turns black. It is not in an instant that a message is sent.

statement: The grey-to-black delay is a hint (not proof) that Slack most probably does not send messages over WebSocket.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is most probably it is not a WebSocket. Right. That is one hint.

statement: There are three types of communication that can be piggybacked on the same system; depending on the guarantees you want to provide, you pick one over the other. Different guarantees shape the system.
detail: The teacher's examples: Slack (his hypothesis - 'I may be wrong'), WhatsApp (hypothetical) and Zoom chat. The point to grasp is the three types, not the products.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: depending on the guarantees that you want to provide to your users, you would pick one over the other.

statement: Components of the diagram: databases, users, API servers (normal HTTP/REST servers), an 'edge server' - a fancy name for a WebSocket server holding WebSocket connections to users - and a broker like Kafka.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, edge server, I'm just naming it fancy, but it is basically a WebSocket server.

statement: Type 1 (Slack): guarantee that a message is broadcast only after it is persisted; unless it is saved it should not be sent to anyone.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I want to provide guarantees like when my message persists, then only I will broadcast.

statement: Broadcasting a message without persisting it may be okay for normal users chatting on Instagram, but is a very bad experience for an enterprise application where communication is key.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It is okay to do it with normal user like you and me on Instagram chatting, but not on an enterprise application...

statement: Sending a message to everyone without ensuring persistence causes loss of credibility: people can misquote you ('I received this message, see it right here').
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then there is a loss of credibility. Why? Because then people can misquote you.

statement: Slack flow (synchronous persistence): the user sends the message over HTTP to an API server; the API server persists it in the database; the API server then sends the message/event to the WebSocket server, which delivers it to users in real time.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: making a call to API server, persisting the message, API server sending the message to WebSocket server

statement: For Slack: send over normal HTTP, receive over WebSocket (so the user doesn't have to refresh the page) - a good experience that ensures the message is persisted before it reaches anyone.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So sending normal HTTP, receiving over WebSocket, because that's a good experience.

statement: Type 2 (hypothetical WhatsApp): when you send a WhatsApp message it is stored on your local mobile, so one copy is always on the user's device; suppose (hypothetically - WhatsApp does not do this) WhatsApp also wanted to store messages in a backend.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In WhatsApp, when you type a message and you send, the message is stored on your local mobile.

statement: If WhatsApp took Slack's synchronous route (HTTP call, database write, then back to the WebSocket server, then the user) it would be far too slow; WhatsApp is meant to be very fast real-time chat, not an enterprise application.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's so slow. WhatsApp is meant to be very fast real time chat. It's not an enterprise application.

statement: Type 2 flow ('green line'): the message is sent from the user over WebSocket to the edge server, which sends it directly to the other user in real time and pushes it onto Kafka, from where it is later (asynchronously) stored in the database; persistence is not guaranteed right away.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This message is just pushed onto Kafka later to be stored in database.

statement: Benefit of type 2: no synchronous database call; writes can be batched through the asynchronous medium while users still get a real-time experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can do batch write through asynchronous medium over here and still give real-time user experience to your user.

statement: In type 2 the message is sent over the WebSocket because it must be real time and the connection is already open anyway.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now because the connection is already open, now we will use it.

statement: Why asynchronous persistence is a bad idea for Slack: Slack users can refresh a channel and read messages from the database; if persisting through Kafka took e.g. 10 minutes, users notified of a message would refresh and not see it. WhatsApp users do not read other messages from the backend, so it works there.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say it takes 10 minutes for you to persist the message in the DB. Imagine Slack.

statement: Different guarantees, different architecture: what is a bad idea for Slack is fine for WhatsApp.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So bad idea to do this with Slack, but on WhatsApp, it is open, and different guarantees, different architecture.

statement: Type 3 (Zoom chat): no persistence at all, only real time; a user sends a message and everyone connected at that moment (e.g. in the meeting) gets it, and that's it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Zoom chat is a classic example. Zoom chat has zero persistence.

statement: On Zoom chat, if you leave and come back in, you do not see historical messages: you only see messages while you are online, because Zoom chat has no backend storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you go out, you come back in, you don't see historical messages on Zoom chat.

statement: Depending on the level of persistence required, pick one way or the other; build this intuition rather than being ingrained that there is only one way ('if I have WebSocket, let me just send it over it').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So depending on the varying level of persistence, you are picking one way or the other.

statement: Avoid database calls from the WebSocket (edge) server: it already handles a ton of TCP connections, and since it is open on the internet, holding a database connection string there is a security problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This WebSocket server is open on the internet, having connections string to the database, security problem.

statement: Making calls directly from the WebSocket server to the database puts a lot of load on that server; you see where it falters when you deploy it and see it in action (infrastructure side).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: making calls directly from WebSocket server to database puts a lot of load on this server.

statement: A lot of companies never put complex logic on the WebSocket server: it just relays messages/events, at most ingesting messages into an asynchronous queue.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why a lot of companies never puts any complex logic on the WebSocket server. They just do relay of messages, of events, that's it.

statement: No one stops you from making a DB call on the WebSocket server, but you avoid it because of security, server load, and because if it goes down it breaks the entire real-time communication of the platform.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because if this goes down, it broke, it breaks the entire real-time communication features of your platform

statement: A student proposed sending messages over UDP over TLS (receiving over WebSocket, retrying until the WebSocket confirms the message reached the server), since HTTPS connections are more resource heavy.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: the guarantees are slim, retries would be much higher, and the client would have to take care of the broadcast instead of the server.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Imagine how many times would you want to retry? The guarantees are very slim.

statement: The server, not the client, should be the one doing the broadcast: if A sends to B over UDP, nothing tells B that the message is there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're doing it over UDP, then who will tell B that the message is there now?

statement: Weigh pros versus cons: micro-optimizations like UDP give a small overhead saving but add retry complexity and needlessly complex client code - don't overcomplicate; when you open Slack you see gRPC requests being fired, no fancy implementation.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you open it, you see gRPC request getting fired there. You don't see any based fancy implementation, right?

statement: Use UDP where it is okay to drop data, not for critical use cases like Slack's message persistence.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would use UDP when you're doing very high in the ocean, where it is okay for you to drop data

statement: Keep systems simple: simple systems are harder to build, but simple systems scale; unnecessary complexity stops scaling and makes the system harder to debug, harder to onboard engineers onto, harder to change, and kills extensibility.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: FYI, simple systems are harder to build, and keep it really simple because simple systems scale.

statement: A student asked whether WebSockets do not offer persistence; the teacher clarified that WebSocket gives a persistent connection, not database persistence, and database persistence is what matters for Slack; doing it via WebSocket means the WebSocket server talks to the database, adding load to a server already balancing many TCP connections, security implications, risk of overwhelming it, and if it goes down the real-time backbone breaks.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, it does give you persistent connection, persistence, not database persistence.

statement: The teacher never lets the WebSocket server talk to the database; at most it puts a message into Kafka, holding only a Kafka connection string.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I never prefer my WebSocket server to talk to database, ever. I never do that.

statement: Edge servers are typically the most vulnerable servers in your infrastructure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: edge servers are typically most vulnerable servers in your infrastructure.

statement: Keep database credentials as secure as possible: if an edge server talks directly to the database it almost exposes the credentials on the internet, and if it gets compromised you are gone; with only a Kafka connection string, basic security holds even on a breach. Database writes belong on a backend server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if this gets compromised, you are gone.

statement: 'Edge server' here does not mean CloudFront edge servers; it means the normal servers on which WebSocket connections are established, a standard terminology.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And when I say edge server, it's not CloudFront edge servers.

statement: Receiving always happens over WebSocket; otherwise the client would have to continuously short-poll and refresh the page.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: receiving will always happen over WebSocket, otherwise you would have to continuously do short polling and refresh the page.

statement: The asynchronous Kafka route is also possible for Slack; the teacher's final diagram uses a Kafka-based implementation even though he prefers the synchronous route here - any implementation is possible depending on guarantees.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In my final diagram, I've done it with Kafka, but any implementation is possible.

statement: With experience you realize every system can be built in 10 different ways; you pick one depending on the guarantees.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can build every system in 10 different ways.

statement: The teacher deliberately keeps designs conflicting and never converges to one design, so that students think about every single decision they take.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's why I deliberately keep it conflicting so that it keeps you, it basically makes you think about every single decision that you are taking.

statement: Next topic: scaling WebSocket servers, one of the most interesting parts; it starts with very basic assumptions whose numbers can be changed to mimic real-world cases.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can just change the number and make it a big... you can just mimic the real world cases.

statement: Whenever a company uses WebSockets (or any persistent connection), the features driven through them are its most critical ones, e.g. Discord chat or video streaming; if the WebSocket servers are gone, real-time chat stops working.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Anytime a product has a persistent connection, it implies that it is powering the most critical features out of it.

statement: Why persistent connections power critical features: the expensive TCP connection persisted between client and backend gives low-latency communication because it does not have to be re-established every time, making the product experience rich.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because now you don't have to reestablish connection every time. This makes your product experience very rich.

statement: Every WebSocket server, like every other server, has a limit on the number of connections it can handle; for the explanation assume the limit is four (in reality much more).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: even a WebSocket server has a limit of number of connections it can handle, right.

statement: Running example: channel 1 has five users A, B, C, D and E; when A sends a message on channel 1, B, C, D and E must all receive it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in which I have 5 users: A, B, C, D and E.

statement: With the four-connection limit, A, B, C and D fill WebSocket server 1, so user E connects to a second server, WebSocket server 2; these are persistent WebSocket connections for high-performance, low-latency communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say a WebSocket server 2 on which your user E is getting connected.

statement: A WebSocket server (e.g. built with Socket.io or an equivalent library) knows which users are connected to it, through the handshake.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in Socket IO the WebSocket server knows who is connected to me.

statement: If you have never written a hello world with Socket.io, do write it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you have ever written hello world with Socket IO; if not, do write it.

statement: When a user connects to a WebSocket server, after establishing the connection it first sends meta information - its membership, i.e. which channels it is part of (e.g. A: channels C1, C2, C3); a message is sent to a channel, not to users.
detail: One option mentioned: the WebSocket server caches the channel information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And then it sends the meta information, meta information like A says, I am part of channel one.

statement: Each WebSocket server keeps (in memory, or maybe on disk) which users are connected to it and which channels they belong to: WS1 knows A, B, C, D are in channel 1; WS2 knows E is in channel 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WebSocket server keeps this information in memory, or maybe storing it in disk, whatever, it's okay, right?

statement: The WebSocket server is kept eventually consistent with membership information: whenever a user joins or leaves a channel the information is sent to it, and users periodically resend their membership meta information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Also, WebSocket server is kept in eventually consistent state with the membership information.

statement: Delivery within one server: A sends a message intended for channel 1 to WS1; WS1 looks up who is in channel 1 (A, B, C, D), skips the sender, and sends the message to B, C and D.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So A sent a message, I would not send it back. I want to send message to B, C, D.

statement: Problem: E is also in channel 1 but connected to another WebSocket server, so the message must somehow reach E on WS2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But now E is also part of the channel. How would he receive the message?

statement: Cross-server delivery is like a group of friends having fun in one hotel room while two friends are in another room: how would they know what you are doing and be part of the fun?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you all group of friends are in one room, in one hotel room, two of your friends are in another hotel room.

statement: A student proposed routing the message through the API server connected to both WebSocket servers (noting it would be slow); the teacher did not take it up and pushed for how the message gets from WS1 to WS2.

statement: When stuck, go to first principles: ask how to even approach an unknown situation like this.

statement: A student proposed a messaging service such as Kafka between the WebSocket servers.

statement: A student proposed another server connecting the two WebSocket servers to relay a replica of the message.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: why another server - these two machines can talk to each other directly, you create TCP connections all the time.
speaker: student (proposal)

statement: Solution: WS1 establishes one plain TCP connection (not a WebSocket connection) with WS2 and relays the message over it; WS2 sees the message is for channel 1, looks up which of its users want channel 1 (E), and sends it to E.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just create a normal TCP server, may not be, it doesn't have the WebSocket connection, normal TCP connection.

statement: A TCP connection between two machines is the bare minimum when you want them to talk; don't introduce more complexity than that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is a bare, bare minimum that you have to do when you want two machines to talk to each other.

statement: Each WebSocket server then has WebSocket connections for all its connected users plus one TCP connection to talk to another WebSocket server; this solves the problem - B, C, D and E all receive channel 1's message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have one WebSocket connection for all the users connected and one TCP connection to talk to another WebSocket server.

statement: Adding a third server: user F joins channel 1 but connects to WS3; WS1 also builds a TCP connection to WS3, so A's message goes to B, C, D locally, to E via WS2 and to F via WS3 - everyone in channel C1 gets it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say this is WS3 and I have a user F which has now joined this channel

statement: How to approach any problem: start with the problem, solve it with basic fundamentals, then think about making it better.
speaker: teacher

statement: Connecting servers this way forms a mesh: every WebSocket server has to be connected to every other WebSocket server, no matter how many servers there are.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every WebSocket server has to be connected to every other WebSocket server.

statement: A student said the mesh's overhead is that each server must keep all those connections alive and re-establish any that die; the teacher asked why that is an overhead and kept probing.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: each server is responsible for making sure that all those connections stay alive.

statement: A student said each message is sent to every server even if it does not need it.

statement: Focusing on a minor issue while missing the real overhead is like worrying about a small mouse while a dinosaur behind you is staring at you.

statement: Before jumping into a solution, first understand and explain the actual problem (three people used the word 'overhead' but no one explained what it is).

statement: Server discovery when horizontally scaling WebSocket servers is a different problem, not the mesh overhead.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, that's a different problem. But that's still not an overhead, overhead.

statement: A student said one connection per WebSocket server limits horizontal scaling since a server can't have infinite connections.
detail: Correction: The teacher countered that a server can still have a good amount (say a million), there would never be more than 10,000 servers, and 10,000 connections are created with ease - but called this answer the closest.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Or anyway, I would not have more than 10,000 servers. I can create 10,000 connections with ease.

statement: A student thought every message to another WebSocket server needs a three-way handshake.
detail: Correction: The teacher corrected it: the TCP connection is established once and messages are just relayed over it, not re-established for every message.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Once, once the TCP connection is established, you don't, you just relay the message over it.

statement: Every server has a limited number of ports on which it can accept connections, so WebSocket servers have a limited capacity for WebSocket connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: obviously every server has a limited number of ports on which it can accept the connections.

statement: The real overhead of the mesh: every WebSocket server hogs persistent TCP connections just to stay connected to every other server; e.g. with a 4-user server and 3 peer servers, 7 connections, of which 3 are only for inter-server communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm having seven connections out of which three are just for inter-server communication.

statement: A WebSocket server's job is to serve users; the mesh architecture wastes many of its TCP connections just talking among servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are wasting a lot of TCP connections to just talk to, to just talk among the servers.
